title: Connection pooling and database limits
subtitle: Learn why databases run out of connections, how to size and guard a pool, and what breaks when you put PgBouncer in front of Postgres.

c.v: On 30 October 2026, some requests to github.com hung for up to about 10 seconds. Then they failed with a server error. At the worst point, about 43% of
merge attempts failed. About 3.5% of API calls failed too.
, not the database itself. A pool used by many github.com services had reached its limit. For several minutes, no connections were available.

The pool was already near its limit. Then some update requests began to hold their connections far longer than expected. Each one started writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds. During that lookup, the connection was "reserved but unused".

GitHub changed the order. The slow lookup now runs before the write starts, so it holds no connection. GitHub is also looking at limits on how long a pooled connection can be held.
A database connection is expensive to open and expensive to keep. So apps open a few, keep them, and lend them out. That set of reusable connections is a
A pool is a tiny resource with a queue in front of it. A request borrows a connection, uses it and gives it back. If all connections are out, the next request waits. If it waits too long, it fails.
So a pool works only if two things are true. The pool is the right size. And every borrower gives the connection back quickly.
The database can serve only a few connections well. Keep pools small, count them across every app instance, and hold a connection only while you are actually talking to the database.

Why not just raise it to 5,000? Memory is not the main problem. Andres Freund measured idle connections at below 2 MiB each with a good setup.
The real cost is that every open connection makes the others slower. In tests he published in 2020, a single active connection ran less than half as fast with 5,000 mostly idle connections open.
Few connections, kept busy, beat many idle ones.

How big? Smaller than you think. HikariCP's "About Pool Sizing" page describes an Oracle demo. Cutting the pool from 2,048 connections to 96 cut response times from about 100 ms to about 2 ms.
A database server has a few CPU cores. Beyond some point, more connections only add switching and waiting.

External poolers: PgBouncer and RDS Proxy
PgBouncer can accept many client connections and share a few server connections among them. It has three pooling modes:
A client keeps one server connection until it disconnects. Every Postgres feature works. It is the default.

Pool exhaustion looks strange from the outside. The app is slow and returns errors. But the database CPU is low and its queries are fast. The time is spent waiting for a connection, not running a query.
The acquire timeout is your safety valve. A 30-second default means callers hang for 30 seconds first.

q.v: Your service has 25 pods, each with a fixed-size pool of 10 (HikariCP's default). Postgres has max_connections = 300. What happens during a deploy that briefly runs 40 pods?

options.v: Nothing. Pools only open connections when they need them.
The pods need 400 connections, more than the server allows, so some fail to connect.
Postgres queues the extra connections until others close.

why.v: Each pod has its own pool. 25 × 10 = 250 fits, but 40 × 10 = 400 is over the limit, and 3 slots are reserved for superusers.

q.v: A request starts a transaction, calls a payment API for 4 seconds, then commits. What is the main pool problem?

options.v: It holds a connection for 4 seconds while doing no database work.
The payment API call uses up the database's CPU.
Nothing, as long as the pool is large.

why.v: The connection is borrowed but idle. A few of these requests can take the whole pool, as in GitHub's October 2026 incident.

q.v: You move from direct connections to PgBouncer in transaction mode. Which code is most likely to break?

options.v: A plain SELECT inside BEGIN and COMMIT.
A job that takes a session-level advisory lock, then runs several transactions.
An INSERT with a RETURNING clause.

why.v: Session-level advisory locks are not supported in transaction pooling. The next transaction may run on a different server connection.

why.v: HikariCP logs a possible leak when a connection has been out of the pool longer than this threshold. It is off by default.
